newsitem.title: UK: UK's new financial watchdog chief eyes ex-mutuals.
newsitem.headline: UK's new financial watchdog chief eyes ex-mutuals.

text.p: Howard Davies, set to become head of Britain's revamped Securities Investment Board (SIB), said on Thursday one of his main concerns was institutions delving into areas in which they had little experience or expertise.

"The sorts of things that worry me are institutions moving into areas of business about which they know little; areas that look exciting, look like fun and look as though there is money to be made out of them," Davies said in an interview in the Guardian newspaper.

Under the new SIB, cash-rich former building societies and insurance companies would come under close scrutiny in an attempt to prevent them squandering the proceeds of their stock market flotations, said the Guardian.

Britain's Labour government overhauled the financial watchdog system soon after it came to power in elections in May, setting up a super-regulator intended to provide more active scrutiny of the financial sector.
Davies, currently deputy governor of the Bank of England, takes over as head of the SIB next month.

"The building societies who are now banks and want to move into other areas of banking -- that is an area to watch," Davies said. "Have they equipped themselves properly, do they know enough about it?"

He added: "The traditional borderline between financial institutions has blurred and almost disappeared. Insurance companies are now owning banks, supermarkets are owning banks, banks are thinking about owning insurance companies. It's all in areas where people haven't grown up (in that sector). They haven't built their business from the bottom."

The newspaper said Davies was anxious that City firms were increasing their exposure by using remuneration strategies that encouraged risk-taking, adding to the dangers inherent in cut-throat competition.
Davies identified two specific pitfalls that could ensnare City firms over the next couple of years, the Guardian said.

"I would like institutions to stress-test their portfolios. There are lots of EMU plays at the moment, but what happens if it doesn't go ahead? Firms should also ask themselves whether they are millennium-compliant," Davies said.
